You said: Octane api query
To query data using the OpenText ALM Octane REST API, you append a query parameter to your standard GET requests on an entity collection. 
The base structure of an Octane API query looks like this:
GET https://<server>/api/shared_spaces/<space_id>/workspaces/<workspace_id>/?query="<field> <operator> <value>" 
🔑 Key Query Operators
Octane uses specific text-based operators rather than mathematical symbols: 
  • EQ: Equal to
  • NE: Not equal to
  • GT / GE: Greater than / Greater than or equal to
  • LT / LE: Less than / Less than or equal to
  • IN: Matches any value in a comma-separated list 
📝 Common Query Examples
Here is how you format your query syntax for different data types. Note that the entire query string value must be URL-encoded when transmitted over HTTP. 
1. Simple Field Filtering 
Filter for defects with a status of "New". String values with special characters or spaces can be wrapped in carets (^) or single quotes: 
http
?query="status EQ ^New^"
Use code with caution.
2. Numeric and ID Filtering 
Find items with an internal ID greater than a specific threshold: 
http
?query="id GT 293087"
Use code with caution.
3. Cross-Filtering (Relational Data) 
To query fields belong to a related entity (like finding defects assigned to a specific release ID), wrap the sub-query in curly braces {}: 
http
?query="release={id EQ 1001}"
Use code with caution.
4. Logical Operators (AND / OR) 
  • AND (using ;): Find critical defects that are also new.
    http
    ?query="severity EQ ^Critical^;status EQ ^New^"
    Use code with caution.
  • OR (using ||): Find items assigned to either of two specific users.
    http
    ?query="owner={id EQ 2001} || owner={id EQ 2002}"
    Use code with caution.
     
⚡ Best Practices for Performance
  • Limit Fields: Use &fields=id,name,status to only return properties you need rather than the full entity payload.
  • Limit Expansions: Avoid expanding (&expand=...) more than two or three relational fields per request to prevent slowdowns.
  • URL Encoding: Always URL-encode your query parameter. For example, query="id GT 100" becomes query=%22id%20GT%20100%22. 
To help build the exact request context you need, please let me know: 
  • Which entity are you trying to query? (e.g., defects, manual tests, user stories, requirements)
  • What specific filters or conditions do you want to apply?
  • Which programming language or tool (like Python, Java, or Postman) are you using to make the API call?

You said: I want to query defects by owner. how to query using api?
To query defects by their owner in OpenText ALM Octane, you filter by the relational owner field using its internal object structure. 
Here is the direct query syntax to use in your API request: 
http
GET https://<server>/api/shared_spaces/<space_id>/workspaces/<workspace_id>/defects?query="owner={id EQ <user_id>}"
Use code with caution.
📋 Examples by Identifier Type
Depending on whether you have the owner's unique numeric ID or their email/name, you can structure your query in a few different ways: 
1. Query by User ID (Recommended) 
This is the fastest and most reliable method because internal database IDs never change. 
http
?query="owner={id EQ 2001}"
Use code with caution.
2. Query by User Name or Email 
If you only know the person's login name or email address, query the nested name attribute of the owner entity. Wrap the email in carets (^) to handle special symbols safely: 
http
?query="owner={name EQ ^john.doe@company.com^}"
Use code with caution.
3. Query Multiple Owners (OR Logic) 
To find defects assigned to any one of a group of people, use the || operator inside the brackets: 
http
?query="owner={id EQ 2001 || id EQ 2002}"
Use code with caution.
4. Find Unassigned Defects 
To see all defects that currently have no owner assigned, look for an empty reference: 
http
?query="owner EQ null"
Use code with caution.
💡 Implementation Tip
Always remember to URL-encode your query parameter before sending the request. For example, ?query="owner={id EQ 2001}" becomes: 
text
?query=%22owner%3D%7Bid%20EQ%202001%7D%22
Use code with caution.

You said: I want to find defects owned by multiple users.
To find defects owned by multiple users in ALM Octane, you use the logical || (OR) operator inside the owner entity brackets, or use the IN operator for a list of IDs. 
Here are the two best ways to structure your query parameter: 
1. Using the IN Operator (Cleanest)
The IN operator lets you pass a comma-separated list of IDs inside the relational brackets. This is the most efficient method when you have a list of user IDs. 
http
?query="owner={id IN 2001,2002,2003}"
Use code with caution.
2. Using the || (OR) Operator
If you are filtering by usernames, emails, or prefer explicit conditions, use the || operator inside the curly braces. 
  • By User ID:
    http
    ?query="owner={id EQ 2001 || id EQ 2002 || id EQ 2003}"
    Use code with caution.
  • By Email / Username:
    Wrap names containing special characters like dots or @ signs in carets (^):
    http
    ?query="owner={name EQ ^user.one@company.com^ || name EQ ^user.two@company.com^}"
    Use code with caution.
     
⚠️ URL Encoding Warning
Because these queries use special characters like spaces, curly braces, and vertical pipes, they must be URL-encoded before transmission. 
The encoded version of the IN query looks like this: 
text
?query=%22owner%3D%7Bid%20IN%202001%2C2002%2C2003%7D%22
Use code with caution.

      You said: In my Angular web app, I want to call Octane API to get all defects or other objects from Octane. Here're something I prepared. - in .env, I configured the OCTANE_API_URL, OCTANE_API_CLINET_ID, OCTANE_API_SECRET - in assets/config/octane-query.json, I put all my queries as below. { "queries": [ { "name": "defects_qry_by_id", "collections": "defects", "fields": "detected_by, owner", "query": "\"id IN 2085565, 2266606\"" }, { "name": "defects_qry_by_owners", "collections": "defects", "fields": "detected_by, owner", "query": "\"owner={full_name IN 'Daniel Fischer', 'Vincent Yin'}\"" } ] } - As the API client id and secret are provided, I assume there should be no constraints of web app hosting. Data can be retreived from any web hosts.
      Before looking at the Angular code, we must address a critical security flaw in your architectural plan, followed by an immediate syntax correction for your JSON file. 
      🛑 Crucial Security Correction
      Your assumption that "Data can be retrieved from any web host because credentials are provided" is highly unsafe. 
      Angular is a client-side framework. Every piece of code, including environmental variables packaged at build time (.env), is shipped directly to the user's web browser. If you use OCTANE_API_CLIENT_ID and OCTANE_API_SECRET directly inside your Angular app: 
      1. Anyone can press F12, open the Network tab, or inspect your source code.
      2. They will steal your Octane Secret Key.
      3. They will gain full API access to your company's internal Octane instance under that API key's permissions. 
      The Solution: You must build a lightweight backend proxy (e.g., using Node.js/Express, .NET, or Java). Your Angular app should call your backend, and your backend will securely hold the secrets, attach them to the headers, call Octane, and return the data to Angular. 
      🔍 Octane JSON Syntax Fix
      Your octane-query.json file has two syntax issues that will cause Octane to reject the requests: 
      1. The full_name field does not exist: Octane user entities do not have a field called full_name. You must use name (which maps to the email/login string) or query by their internal IDs. 
      2. String wrapping inside brackets: When querying multiple names using IN, each string must be wrapped in carets (^) or escaped double quotes, not single quotes. 
      Update your assets/config/octane-query.json to look like this: 
      json
      {
  "queries": [
    {
      "name": "defects_qry_by_id",
      "collections": "defects",
      "fields": "detected_by,owner",
      "query": "\"id IN 2085565,2266606\""
    },
    {
      "name": "defects_qry_by_owners",
      "collections": "defects",        
      "fields": "detected_by,owner",
      "query": "\"owner={name IN ^daniel.fischer@company.com^,^vincent.yin@company.com^}\""
    }
  ]
}
      Use code with caution.
      🛠️ Angular Implementation (via a Secure Backend Proxy)
      Assuming you have routed your requests through a proxy server to keep your API keys hidden, here is the clean, scannable architecture to load your JSON configuration and execute the Octane query using Angular's HttpClient. 
      1. Define the Query Model 
      Create an interface to map your JSON config file cleanly. 
      typescript
      export interface OctaneQueryConfig {
  name: string;
  collections: string;
  fields: string;
  query: string;
}

export interface QueryJsonStructure {
  queries: OctaneQueryConfig[];
}
      Use code with caution.
      2. Create the Data Service 
      This service loads your local JSON configuration asset first, finds the target query profile, builds the HTTP request with the necessary URL encoding, and sends it to your endpoint. 
      typescript
      import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { HttpClient, HttpParams } from '@angular/common/http';
import { Observable, switchMap, map } from 'rxjs';
import { QueryJsonStructure, OctaneQueryConfig } from './octane.models';

@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class OctaneService {
  private configUrl = 'assets/config/octane-query.json';
  
  // Note: This points to your proxy backend, NOT directly to Octane's domain
  private proxyApiBaseUrl = '/api/octane-proxy'; 

  constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}

  /**
   * Loads the local JSON config and finds the target query profile by name
   */
  private getQueryConfig(queryName: string): Observable<OctaneQueryConfig> {
    return this.http.get<QueryJsonStructure>(this.configUrl).pipe(
      map(response => {
        const found = response.queries.find(q => q.name === queryName);
        if (!found) throw new Error(`Query wrapper '${queryName}' not found in JSON config.`);
        return found;
      })
    );
  }

  /**
   * Fetches the defects using the dynamic configurations fetched from JSON
   */
  public getDefectsByProfile(profileName: string): Observable<any> {
    return this.getQueryConfig(profileName).pipe(
      switchMap((config: OctaneQueryConfig) => {
        
        // Strip the outer JSON escaped quotes if they persist
        const cleanQuery = config.query.replace(/^"|"$/g, '');

        // Use HttpParams to safely URL-encode the parameters automatically
        const params = new HttpParams()
          .set('fields', config.fields.replace(/\s+/g, '')) // Remove white spaces
          .set('query', cleanQuery);

        const targetUrl = `${this.proxyApiBaseUrl}/${config.collections}`;

        return this.http.get<any>(targetUrl, { params });
      })
    );
  }
}
      Use code with caution.
      3. Consume in your Component 
      typescript
      import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core';
import { OctaneService } from './octane.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-defect-list',
  template: `
    <div *ngIf="defects.length > 0">
      <div *ngFor="let defect of defects">
        Defect ID: {{ defect.id }} - Owner: {{ defect.owner?.name }}
      </div>
    </div>
  `
})
export class DefectListComponent implements OnInit {
  defects: any[] = [];

  constructor(private octaneService: OctaneService) {}

  ngOnInit() {
    this.octaneService.getDefectsByProfile('defects_qry_by_owners').subscribe({
      next: (data) => this.defects = data.data || [],
      error: (err) => console.error('Failed fetching data', err)
    });
  }
}

          You said: To make it easier, I would like to run scripts locally to retrieve data into .json data files. Then render them in pages.
          Running a local script to download the data into JSON files is a fantastic alternative. It keeps your API credentials safely on your machine and completely bypasses any security risks or complex backend infrastructure. 
          Here is a complete setup to fetch the data locally using a Node.js script, save it to your Angular assets/ folder, and read it natively in your application. 
          🛠️ Step 1: Set Up the Local Fetch Script
          1. Create a file named fetch-octane.js in the root of your project.
          2. Ensure you have axios and dotenv installed in your project (npm install axios dotenv). 
          Add the following code to fetch-octane.js: 
          javascript
          const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const axios = require('axios');
require('dotenv').config();

// Load environments
const baseUrl = process.env.OCTANE_API_URL;
const clientId = process.env.OCTANE_API_CLIENT_ID;
const clientSecret = process.env.OCTANE_API_SECRET;

// Load query templates from your JSON file
const queriesConfig = require('./src/assets/config/octane-query.json');

async function run() {
  try {
    console.log('🔑 Authenticating with ALM Octane...');
    
    // 1. Authenticate and get a session cookie/token
    const authResponse = await axios.post(`${baseUrl}/authentication/sign_in`, {
      client_id: clientId,
      client_secret: clientSecret
    });
    
    // Store cookies for subsequent requests
    const cookies = authResponse.headers['set-cookie'];

    console.log('🚀 Fetching queries...');

    // 2. Loop through each query inside your config file
    for (const item of queriesConfig.queries) {
      console.log(`Processing: ${item.name}...`);

      // Clean outer quotes from your JSON config
      const cleanQuery = item.query.replace(/^"|"$/g, '');

      // Build destination endpoint URL
      const url = `${baseUrl}/${item.collections}`;

      // Execute request with proper URL parameters
      const response = await axios.get(url, {
        headers: { Cookie: cookies },
        params: {
          fields: item.fields.replace(/\s+/g, ''), // Strip spaces
          query: cleanQuery
        }
      });

      // 3. Save the resulting payload locally in the assets directory
      const fileName = `${item.name}.json`;
      const filePath = path.join(__dirname, 'src', 'assets', 'data', fileName);

      // Ensure directory exists
      fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(filePath), { recursive: true });
      
      // Save data array or the whole structure
      fs.writeFileSync(filePath, JSON.stringify(response.data.data || [], null, 2));
      console.log(`✅ Saved data to: src/assets/data/${fileName}`);
    }

    // 4. Clean up sign out
    await axios.post(`${baseUrl}/authentication/sign_out`, {}, { headers: { Cookie: cookies } });
    console.log('🔒 Logged out successfully.');

  } catch (error) {
    console.error('❌ Error executing fetch script:', error.message);
    if (error.response) console.error('Details:', error.response.data);
  }
}

run();
          Use code with caution.
          📦 Step 2: Automate the Extraction
          You can add a shortcut script into your root package.json file to run this utility smoothly before booting up or building your app: 
          json
          "scripts": {
  "ng": "ng",
  "start": "ng serve",
  "build": "ng build",
  "fetch-data": "node fetch-octane.js"
}
          Use code with caution.
          Now, whenever you run npm run fetch-data, it will scrape Octane and overwrite your local JSON files. 
          💻 Step 3: Render the Static Files in Angular
          Because the files live right inside your public assets/data/ folder, you don't need any complex query strings or authentication logic inside Angular anymore. You just make a basic layout request using HttpClient. 
          1. Update your Service 
          typescript
          import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { Observable } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class DefectDataService {
  constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}

  /**
   * Reads the generated snapshot data from local assets folder
   */
  public getDefectsFromSnapshot(queryName: string): Observable<any[]> {
    return this.http.get<any[]>(`assets/data/${queryName}.json`);
  }
}
          Use code with caution.
          2. Update your Component template 
          typescript
          import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core';
import { DefectDataService } from './defect-data.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-defect-dashboard',
  template: `
    <h2>Octane Defects Snapshot</h2>
    
    <div *ngIf="defects.length === 0">No tracking defects found in local cache.</div>

    <table border="1" *ngIf="defects.length > 0">
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th>ID</th>
          <th>Owner Name</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr *ngFor="let defect of defects">
          <td>{{ defect.id }}</td>
          <td>{{ defect.owner?.name || 'Unassigned' }}</td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  `
})
export class DefectDashboardComponent implements OnInit {
  defects: any[] = [];

  constructor(private dataService: DefectDataService) {}

  ngOnInit() {
    // Matches the "name" property inside your octane-query.json configuration mapping
    this.dataService.getDefectsFromSnapshot('defects_qry_by_owners').subscribe({
      next: (data) => this.defects = data,
      error: (err) => console.error('Could not load local static JSON data file', err)
    });
  }
}

          octane-prod.bmwgroup.netFile has been removed
          The API URL is like https://octane-prod.bmwgroup.net/api/shared_spaces/1002/workspaces/2001/defects?...Shall I split it into base url and other part?
          Yes, you absolutely should split the URL. 
          Octane requires you to hit different URL structures for authentication versus fetching data, and separating them makes your script much cleaner and less prone to string concatenation errors. 
          Here is the best practice method to split your URL and update your script layout. 
          🗺️ How to Split the URL
          Break the path down into three logical parts inside your .env file: 
          ini
          # The base server domain
OCTANE_BASE_URL=https://octane-prod.bmwgroup.net

# The specific workspace context path
OCTANE_WORKSPACE_PATH=/api/shared_spaces/1002/workspaces/2001

# Credentials
OCTANE_API_CLIENT_ID=your_client_id
OCTANE_API_SECRET=your_secret
          Use code with caution.
          🔄 Why is this necessary?
          Your local Node script performs two different operations, which require different URL roots: 
          1. Sign-In/Sign-Out happens at the root server level:
            https://bmwgroup.net
          2. Data Queries happen inside your workspace path:
            https://octane-prod.bmwgroup.net/api/shared_spaces/1002/workspaces/2001/defects             
          If you do not split the URL, you would have to write complex string manipulation logic to strip out the workspace numbers just to log in. 
          🛠️ Updated Node.js Script Implementation
          Here is how to adapt your fetch-octane.js script to use these split environment variables cleanly: 
          javascript
          const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const axios = require('axios');
require('dotenv').config();

// Load the newly split configuration elements
const baseUrl = process.env.OCTANE_BASE_URL;
const workspacePath = process.env.OCTANE_WORKSPACE_PATH;
const clientId = process.env.OCTANE_API_CLIENT_ID;
const clientSecret = process.env.OCTANE_API_SECRET;

const queriesConfig = require('./src/assets/config/octane-query.json');

async function run() {
  try {
    console.log('🔑 Authenticating with ALM Octane...');
    
    // Auth endpoints sit directly under the base server domain root
    const authResponse = await axios.post(`${baseUrl}/authentication/sign_in`, {
      client_id: clientId,
      client_secret: clientSecret
    });
    
    const cookies = authResponse.headers['set-cookie'];
    console.log('🚀 Authentication successful. Fetching queries...');

    for (const item of queriesConfig.queries) {
      console.log(`Processing: ${item.name}...`);

      const cleanQuery = item.query.replace(/^"|"$/g, '');

      // Combine base, workspace path, and the specific collection name (e.g., defects)
      const targetUrl = `${baseUrl}${workspacePath}/${item.collections}`;

      const response = await axios.get(targetUrl, {
        headers: { Cookie: cookies },
        params: {
          fields: item.fields.replace(/\s+/g, ''),
          query: cleanQuery
        }
      });

      const fileName = `${item.name}.json`;
      const filePath = path.join(__dirname, 'src', 'assets', 'data', fileName);

      fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(filePath), { recursive: true });
      fs.writeFileSync(filePath, JSON.stringify(response.data.data || [], null, 2));
      console.log(`✅ Saved data to: src/assets/data/${fileName}`);
    }

    // Sign out uses the base server domain root
    await axios.post(`${baseUrl}/authentication/sign_out`, {}, { headers: { Cookie: cookies } });
    console.log('🔒 Session closed safely.');

  } catch (error) {
    console.error('❌ Error executing fetch script:', error.message);
    if (error.response) console.error('Details:', error.response.data);
  }
}

run();

              Your current script is already perfectly set up to accept our task! Because your pipeline uses Promise.all() to run tasks in parallel, we don't need to change any of your core execution logic. 
              We only need to map your new fetch-octane task to a flag (e.g., --octane) and ensure it gets included when the --all master flag is triggered. 
              Here is your updated run-pipeline-async.js file: 
              javascript
              const { exec } = require('child_process');

// Capture arguments passed after the script name
const args = process.argv.slice(2); 

// Helper to execute npm scripts asynchronously with Promise tracking
function runScriptAsync(scriptName) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    console.log(`🚀 Started: npm run ${scriptName}...`);
    
    // Launch process. Output is piped to parent process streams to maintain real-time logs.
    const child = exec(`npm run ${scriptName}`);

    child.stdout.pipe(process.stdout);
    child.stderr.pipe(process.stderr);

    child.on('exit', (code) => {
      if (code === 0) {
        console.log(`\n✅ Script ${scriptName} completed successfully.`);
        resolve();
      } else {
        reject(new Error(`❌ Script ${scriptName} failed with exit code ${code}.`));
      }
    });
  });
}

async function main() {
  const tasksToRun = [];

  // Determine which scripts need to be queued up based on flags
  if (args.includes('--all')) {
    // 💡 Added 'fetch-octane' to the master task list
    tasksToRun.push('fetch-data', 'generate-docs-tree', 'fetch-jira', 'fetch-octane');
  } else {
    if (args.includes('--data')) tasksToRun.push('fetch-data');
    if (args.includes('--docs')) tasksToRun.push('generate-docs-tree');
    if (args.includes('--jira')) tasksToRun.push('fetch-jira');
    // 💡 Added a dedicated standalone flag for Octane tasks
    if (args.includes('--octane')) tasksToRun.push('fetch-octane');
  }

  // Handle accidental flag-less executions
  if (tasksToRun.length === 0) {
    console.warn('⚠️ Warning: No valid flags provided. No pre-build tasks executed.');
    process.exit(0);
  }

  try {
    // Map script names into array of promises and execute them in parallel
    const promises = tasksToRun.map(script => runScriptAsync(script));
    await Promise.all(promises);
    
    console.log('\n🎉 All pre-build tasks completed successfully!');
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(`\n${error.message}`);
    // Fail immediately so npm stop the execution chain (e.g., stops ng build or ng serve)
    process.exit(1); 
  }
}

main();
